b: The client gifts people remember are personal, useful, or unexpected. For holiday gifts, start with what you know about each client, check their company’s gift policy, keep your logo small, and ship early so your gift arrives before mid-December. And watch for moments outside the holidays, like a birthday or a hard week, when a small gesture can mean even more.
Choose each gift around the person, not one gift for your whole list.
A small, well-timed gift can turn a brush-off into a closed deal.
Some of the most memorable gifts come outside the holiday season.
Check your client’s gift policy before you send anything.
Ship holiday gifts early so they arrive before the rush.
Add a handwritten note to every gift.

Recently, one of our sales trainers was prospecting and trying to book a meeting when the prospect gave him a classic brush-off: “I’m busy.” But he shared more than that. He was on his way to his son’s ninth birthday party.
In that moment, our trainer had two options. He could say, “Have a great day, I’ll reach back out later,” and the prospect would probably forget the call by dinner. Or he could do something more.

The moment he hung up, he sent a $20 LEGO set for the prospect’s son. After the gift arrived, the prospect ended up booking a meeting, and our trainer eventually closed the deal. He didn’t send the gift to win the sale. He sent it because he was actually listening, and the prospect noticed.

Most salespeople think about client gifts once a year, in December. The holidays are a great time to say thank you, but they’re also when your clients get the most gifts from everyone else. The trick is giving gifts that stand out because they feel chosen for that specific person.
The Gifts Clients Remember Are the Ones They Didn’t See Coming

Another one of our sales trainers emailed a client and got an out-of-office reply: the client was out for surgery. The trainer sent flowers and a get-well card. The card didn’t mention business at all. It simply let the client know someone was thinking about them.

At Sales Gravy, we reference Will Guidara’s book Unreasonable Hospitality often. Guidara, who led the three-Michelin-star restaurant Eleven Madison Park, built its reputation on small, personal surprises. One of the most memorable stories in the book is about a group of guests who mentioned they’d never had a New York street hot dog. His team went out, bought one, and served it to them at the table. The same idea works in sales. When you pay attention to what people tell you, you’ll find chances to do something thoughtful they never expected.

These moments don’t happen on a schedule. Listen for them on calls and in emails, and watch for birthdays, promotions, new babies, and hard weeks. A small gift at the right moment can mean much more than an expensive one in December.
How to Choose a Holiday Gift for Your Clients
When you’re sending gifts to a whole list of clients, it’s tempting to order 50 of the same thing. Take a few extra minutes per client instead.
Start With What You Know About Them

Look back at your notes and your recent conversations. If a client mentioned a golf trip, a new puppy, or their favorite coffee shop, start there. If you want to send food, stay away from major allergens (nuts, dairy, gluten) if you don’t know their dietary preferences.

Do not send them something that will end up in a donation box a month later. It is very tempting to opt for the cheaper, low-quality option to save a few dollars, but when you send them something useless, they will remember that. If you know they have a pet, send them treats. Or if you know they love taking handwritten notes, send a high-quality notebook and pen.

Many companies, especially in government, healthcare, and financial services, limit what employees can accept. Be aware of their policies before sending anything, especially if it is expensive. A client having to return your gift is far more awkward than no gift at all.

If you want to put your logo on an item, do it intentionally and keep it small. Otherwise, it will feel like a marketing tactic instead of real appreciation for their business. Or skip the logo altogether and let the note and gift do the talking.
Everyday items they’ll use: a quality notebook, pen, tumbler, or desk accessory with a subtle logo.
Gifts based on their interests: golf balls for the golfer, a cookbook for the home cook, or gear from their favorite team.
Something for their family: like the LEGO set, a gift for a client’s kids or partner shows you remembered what matters to them.
Food the whole team can share: a box of treats sent to the office, so everyone on the account sees your name.
Experiences: a gift card to a local restaurant, or tickets to a game or show.
A book you think they’d enjoy, with a note about why you picked it.
A donation in their name to a charity they support.
When to Send Holiday Client Gifts

Plan for your gifts to arrive by mid-December. Shipping slows down in December, and plenty of clients take the last week or two of the year off. If you’ll see clients at holiday events this season, consider bringing your gift in person.

If you’d rather stand out, send yours at Thanksgiving or for the New Year, when fewer gifts are showing up on their desk. At Sales Gravy, we like to do Valentine’s Day gifts for clients to show our love for them.
Remember the People Behind the Scenes

The person you work with in the account isn’t the only person who keeps deals moving. If you can, send gifts for the assistant who gets you on the calendar, the coordinator who processes your orders, and the partners who help you deliver.

Writing a handwritten note is the most time-consuming part of sending a gift, and it’s often the part people skip, especially when they outsource the gifts. But every gift you send should come with one. It shows you took the time and is often the part your client remembers most. Keep it short, mention something specific from your year together, and leave out any sales pitch.

Gifts are one way to show clients you’re paying attention. If you want your account managers doing that every day, Account Expansion Selling gives them a proven system to deepen relationships and grow revenue in the accounts you already have.
What are good client gift ideas?

The best client gifts are personal or useful: something tied to their interests, an everyday item they’ll keep on their desk, a gift for their family, food the whole team can share, an experience like a restaurant gift card, or a donation to a charity they support.
What makes a client gift memorable?

Thought and timing. A gift that reflects something your client told you, or arrives at a moment they didn’t expect, like a birthday or a tough week, tends to stick with them far longer than an expensive gift that could have gone to anyone.
How much should you spend on a client gift?

Spend what fits the relationship and your budget, and check your client’s gift policy first, since many companies limit what employees can accept. In the US, business gift deductions are capped at $25 per recipient per year, so check with your accountant about the tax side.
When should you send holiday gifts to clients?
Aim for gifts to arrive by mid-December, before clients leave for the holidays. To stand out, consider sending at Thanksgiving or for the New Year.
When should sales reps use gifting in outbound sequences?

Use gifts sparingly, after you’ve researched the prospect and have a real reason to reach out. A small, relevant gift can help a message stand out, but it should support a conversation, not replace one.
